sources.title: Metformin improves cognitive impairment in patients with schizophrenia: associated with enhanced functional connectivity of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex
sources.population: Clinically stable schizophrenia of at most five years duration; young adults at the Second Xiangya Hospital, China; mean age 22.8 years.
sources.sampleDescription: 72 randomized: metformin plus antipsychotics 48, antipsychotics alone 24. 59 completed 24 weeks. Completion is not the model-analysis denominator.

sources.preview: Adjunctive metformin improved the reported composite cognitive-test score over 24 weeks in this small open-label trial.

effects.population: Clinically stable schizophrenia of at most five years duration; young adults at the Second Xiangya Hospital, China; mean age 22.8 years.
effects.recordedNotes: 72 randomized; 59 completed. Exact number contributing to the mixed-model estimate not separately verified; do not label 59 as the analysis population.

locators.section: Results: Metformin ameliorated cognitive dysfunction as evaluated by the MCCB; Figure 2

effects.sampleDenominatorNote: 72 randomized; 59 completed. Exact number contributing to the mixed-model estimate not separately verified; do not label 59 as the analysis population.
intervention: Metformin 500 mg three times daily added to antipsychotics for 24 weeks

finding.text: Adjunctive metformin improved the reported composite cognitive-test score compared with antipsychotic treatment alone after 24 weeks.

limitations.text: The trial was small and open-label, without placebo; 59 of 72 participants completed follow-up. The practical importance of the score difference remains uncertain.

coverage.scope: One primary trial; not a complete condition-wide synthesis
pending: Formal appraisal and complete supplement review

synthesisRows.evidenceBase: One open-label randomized parent trial; 72 randomized, 59 completed; shared family with CP017.

effects.sampleDenominatorNote: 72 randomized; primary complete-follow-up analysis 70 (34 metformin, 36 placebo). Adjusted treatment effect is not the subtraction of rounded unadjusted arm means.

finding.text: Metformin did not improve walking speed and was poorly tolerated in older adults with probable sarcopenia and prefrailty or frailty.

limitations.text: The trial included 72 participants, predominantly White British, with a mean age of 80.4 years; applicability to younger or less frail populations is limited.
